calls.body: The Wild play some of the league’s fastest games, and so do the Predators. We think this one runs hotter than either team’s usual.

calls.head: The Predators’ edge in depth
calls.body: The Predators are around the middle of the league for depth, and the Wild are near the bottom. It’s the widest gap between these two, though not a huge one.
calls.call: The Predators spread their forward ice time deeper down the lineup than the Wild.

MIN.head: We gave Minnesota a 64% chance, and they delivered.

surprises.head: Minnesota took away the good looks
surprises.body: Minnesota is one of the league’s best at preventing dangerous shots. Even by those standards, this was a night of harmless shots: Nashville’s shots at 5-on-5 had a 3.8% chance of scoring on the average shot, against their usual 6.2% (about 5.9% against Minnesota) and a league average of 6.3%. A team strays this far about once every 25 games.

story.head: The Wild get past the Predators
paras: Blake Coleman made his Wild debut, after five seasons with the Flames. Olli Määttä made his Wild debut, after playing for the Flames, and picked up an assist. Nick Foligno and Coleman scored 4:13 apart midway through the first to put the Wild up 2-0. Minnesota had a goal taken off for goalie interference late in the first. Roman Josi got the Predators on the board midway through the second. Kirill Kaprizov made it 3-1 for the Wild early in the third. They won anyway.

The Wild carried the play, outshooting the Predators 30-20, and got the result to match. Jesper Wallstedt made 19 saves for the Wild, and Juuse Saros stopped 27 of 30. By our Swing measure, Michael McCarron had the best night of anyone.
The Wild killed all four Predators power plays. The Wild improved to 1-0-0, and the Predators dropped to 0-1-0.

items.text: Steven Stamkos extended his point streak against Minnesota to nine games.
The Predators lost their home opener.
This was the first game for both teams since a break.
